questions.question: Moist winds blow from the ocean toward a mountain range. A town on the inland side is much drier than a coastal town at similar elevation. What best explains the difference?

choices.A: Air descending on the inland slope warms and dries after losing moisture on the windward side
choices.B: The inland town receives less rainfall because it is farther from the equator
choices.C: Mountains affect temperature but usually have little effect on precipitation
choices.D: Mountain rain shadows occur because air becomes colder while descending

questions.note: Moist air rises and cools on the windward side; after losing moisture it descends, warms, and tends to produce a drier leeward climate.

questions.question: Two countries have the same land area, but one grows far less food domestically. Which factor most directly explains why area alone cannot predict agricultural capacity?

choices.A: A larger population makes more land available for farming, so area remains a useful stand-alone predictor.
choices.B: Soil, climate, terrain, and reliable water shape how much land can support crops.
choices.C: Countries with similar land area and population density tend to produce similar harvests despite soil and rainfall differences.
choices.D: Domestic food output depends more on market access than on climate, terrain, soil, or water.

questions.note: Total territory is not the same as cultivable land; soil, climate, terrain, and water access affect agricultural potential.

questions.question: A west-coast desert lies beside a cold ocean current and beneath descending subtropical air. Why can these conditions keep rainfall very low?

choices.A: The desert is mainly caused by a mountain rain shadow rather than the stated current and air pattern.
choices.B: The current redirects prevailing winds but has little effect on atmospheric stability.
choices.C: Cool surface water limits evaporation while descending subtropical air suppresses uplift and cloud growth.
choices.D: Cold currents increase evaporation and force moist air upward into persistent rain.

questions.note: Cold currents and subsiding air can suppress convection and rainfall; the Humboldt Current contributes to the Atacama’s aridity.

questions.question: A traveler crosses the International Date Line westward from a place east of the line to a place west of it. Which adjustment is normally required?

choices.A: Westward travel usually subtracts a calendar day because local time becomes earlier.
choices.B: Westward travel across the line normally advances the calendar by one day.
choices.C: Crossing the line changes the local clock, as at an ordinary time-zone boundary, without changing the date.
choices.D: The clock shifts by twelve hours and the calendar date remains unchanged.

questions.note: Crossing the Date Line westward generally advances the calendar date by one day; eastward crossing moves it back one day.

questions.question: A deep, steep-sided coastal inlet has a U-shaped cross-section and a submerged valley extending inland. Which process most likely formed it?

choices.A: A river cut a narrow V-shaped valley that later widened by wave erosion
choices.B: A volcanic cone collapsed and filled with seawater
choices.C: A coral reef grew upward and left a deep central basin
choices.D: A glacier carved a U-shaped valley that was later flooded by the sea

questions.note: Fjords are flooded glacial valleys; their U-shaped cross-sections reflect glacial erosion.

questions.question: A country wants to move goods from its Caribbean port to a Pacific port without crossing an international border. Which geographic condition is required?

choices.A: The country needs an inland river that is navigable from one sea to the other.
choices.B: Its land must reach both seas and provide a route between the two ports.
choices.C: The ports need an inland waterway linking them rather than a road or rail corridor.
choices.D: The country can use an international transit corridor even if one port is beyond its borders.

questions.note: A domestic route between both coasts requires the same country to have access to both seas; Colombia is one example.

questions.question: A ship travels from the Indian Ocean toward East Asia through the narrowest major passage between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra. Why is this route geographically important?

choices.A: The Strait of Malacca is a major trade chokepoint linking Indian Ocean routes with East Asia.
choices.B: The Taiwan Strait links the South China Sea with the East China Sea along the coast of East Asia.
choices.C: Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden near the entrance to the Indian Ocean.
choices.D: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.

questions.note: The Strait of Malacca is a major shipping corridor between the Indian Ocean and East Asian waters, making it strategically important.

questions.question: A river crosses the Equator twice while draining a large basin in Central Africa. What does this course suggest about the river’s path?

choices.A: Its drainage basin spans both sides of the Equator, so the course loops across the line.
choices.B: The basin is mostly in one hemisphere, and the second crossing is caused by the map projection.
choices.C: The river’s source and mouth lie in different hemispheres, requiring a single crossing.
choices.D: The river follows a mostly straight north–south course before reaching the Atlantic.

questions.note: The Congo River crosses the Equator twice, reflecting its broad looping course through Central Africa.

questions.question: A shipment travels west from Brazil toward the Pacific and later enters Chile. Which landlocked country that borders Brazil lies between the two?

choices.A: Peru
choices.B: Paraguay
choices.C: Uruguay
choices.D: Bolivia

questions.note: Bolivia is landlocked, borders Brazil, and lies between Brazil and Chile. Peru and Chile have Pacific coasts; Paraguay is landlocked but does not border Chile.

questions.question: A coastal city and an inland city at the same latitude have similar daytime highs, but the coastal city has milder nights and winters. Which property best explains the pattern?

choices.A: Coastal humidity prevents nighttime radiative cooling regardless of ocean temperature.
choices.B: Sea breezes hold coastal temperatures almost constant from day to day and season to season.
choices.C: Ocean water stores and releases heat more slowly than land, moderating nearby temperatures.
choices.D: Salt in coastal air reflects most incoming sunlight before it reaches the surface.

questions.note: Water’s high heat capacity moderates temperature near coasts, especially seasonal and daily temperature ranges.

questions.question: Two cities lie near 25° north. One is mild and wet; the other is hot and arid. Which comparison best explains why latitude alone is insufficient?

choices.A: Same-latitude places tend to share rainfall patterns, with temperature varying more strongly.
choices.B: Elevation, prevailing winds, ocean currents, and mountain barriers alter local climate.
choices.C: Similar solar angles produce similar moisture supplies, so climate differences mainly reflect measurement conditions.
choices.D: Latitude determines rainfall patterns, while ocean currents mainly influence wind direction.

questions.note: Latitude affects incoming solar energy, but circulation, elevation, proximity to water, and relief strongly affect local climate.

questions.question: A country funds much of its budget by exporting one mineral. The mineral price suddenly falls worldwide. Which vulnerability is most direct?

choices.A: A country selling one mineral is insulated from global price changes if production is steady.
choices.B: A lower price may raise sales volume, but total revenue still depends on demand and supply.
choices.C: Public spending stays stable whenever export tonnage is unchanged.
choices.D: Falling prices can reduce both export earnings and public revenue, limiting spending and jobs.

questions.note: Dependence on one volatile export can transmit global price shocks into government revenue, jobs, and foreign exchange.

questions.question: A country’s GDP rises, but surveys show that poorer provinces experience little income growth. Which explanation best fits both observations?

choices.A: National output can rise while many households’ incomes stagnate, but that pattern means the GDP figures are necessarily miscalculated.
choices.B: Aggregate output can rise while gains are concentrated in particular sectors or regions.
choices.C: GDP growth is unlikely unless most provinces report comparable income gains.
choices.D: GDP directly subtracts regional income inequality from total production, so a rise implies most regions gained.

questions.note: GDP measures total production, not how growth is distributed geographically or across households.

questions.question: A river’s lower course has a broad floodplain and delta, while its upper course is steep and narrow. Which process best explains this change downstream?

choices.A: The river’s gradient usually increases downstream, so the channel becomes wider as vertical erosion intensifies.
choices.B: Sediment deposition dominates upstream, while the lower course mainly transports material without depositing it.
choices.C: The river’s gradient usually decreases, encouraging deposition where flow loses energy
choices.D: The lower course narrows as water approaches sea level because the river loses energy and cuts downward.

questions.note: As gradient and energy generally decline downstream, rivers often shift from valley incision toward lateral erosion, floodplain formation, and sediment deposition.

questions.question: A world map preserves local angles but greatly enlarges high-latitude regions. What should a user conclude before comparing countries’ sizes?

choices.A: A uniform map scale keeps land areas proportional even near the poles.
choices.B: A projection can preserve angles while enlarging high-latitude areas, so area comparisons require care.
choices.C: Preserving local angles also preserves the ratios between the areas of large countries and continents.
choices.D: Projection distortion is concentrated along coastlines, while the relative area of inland regions remains accurate.

questions.note: Map projections trade off properties such as area, shape, distance, and direction; the map’s purpose matters for interpretation.

questions.question: A coastal city pumps groundwater faster than its aquifer recharges. Some wells near the shore gradually become salty. Which process most directly explains the change?

choices.A: As freshwater pressure falls, seawater can move inland into the aquifer and contaminate wells.
choices.B: Evapotranspiration concentrates salt in deep groundwater even when the freshwater–seawater boundary remains stable.
choices.C: River capture redirects seawater through surface drainage into coastal wells, independent of groundwater levels.
choices.D: Coastal erosion raises soil salinity, which then enters deep wells regardless of how much groundwater is pumped.

questions.note: Over-pumping can lower freshwater pressure and allow saline water to intrude into a coastal aquifer.

questions.question: A ship enters the Panama Canal from the Atlantic side at Colón and exits at Balboa on the Pacific side. Why can the overall route trend southeast rather than due west?

choices.A: The canal’s locks redirect ships southeast to compensate for a difference in the Atlantic and Pacific water levels.
choices.B: The Atlantic and Pacific entrances lie on nearly the same longitude, but currents bend ships southeast between them.
choices.C: The southeast trend is a map-projection effect; the canal follows a due-west line on Earth’s surface.
choices.D: The isthmus and its coasts angle southeast toward the Pacific entrance.

questions.note: The canal crosses an angled isthmus: Colón is northwest of Balboa, so the route trends generally southeast.

questions.question: Assume local solar time changes by 1 hour per 15° of longitude. City B is 45° east of City A, and City C is 30° west of City B. How does City C’s local solar time compare with City A’s?

choices.A: 1 hour ahead
choices.B: 5 hours ahead
choices.C: 1 hour behind
choices.D: 5 hours behind

questions.note: City C is 15° east of City A (45° east minus 30° west), so its local solar time is 1 hour ahead. This requires combining both longitude differences and tracking direction.

questions.question: A lake is part of a river basin shared by three countries. One country expands irrigation upstream, and downstream flow drops during the dry season. Which geographic concept is most useful for analyzing the shared problem?

choices.A: A transboundary watershed links upstream land and water use to downstream supply.
choices.B: Political boundaries determine where a river carries its water once it enters a country.
choices.C: A drainage divide explains the limits of a basin, but not allocation within a shared river system.
choices.D: National annual water budgets are sufficient without tracing seasonal flow or withdrawals.

questions.note: Water systems follow drainage basins rather than political borders; upstream withdrawals affect downstream users, especially when flow is seasonal.

questions.question: A point lies at 15° north latitude and 120° east longitude. Ignoring local land features, what are the approximate coordinates of its antipode?
questions.note: The antipode reverses latitude and shifts longitude by 180°: 15° N becomes 15° S, and 120° E becomes 60° W.

questions.question: Two watersheds receive the same intense storm. Basin X has steep slopes, compacted soil, and little vegetation; Basin Y has forest and permeable soils. Why is Basin X more likely to flood quickly?

choices.A: The steepness of a basin affects erosion but not runoff speed
choices.B: Equal rainfall totals usually create equal peak discharge regardless of land cover
choices.C: Less interception and infiltration, along with steep slopes, can increase rapid runoff
choices.D: Forested basins route water to streams more rapidly than compacted soil does

questions.note: Peak flow depends on rainfall intensity, slope, soil permeability, vegetation, and drainage characteristics.

questions.question: A population pyramid has a wide base and a much narrower middle. If fertility stays high, which pressure is most likely to rise first?

choices.A: Demand for secondary education and entry-level jobs would rise before children reach school age.
choices.B: Services for older adults would dominate first because a narrow middle means older adults outnumber children.
choices.C: Demand for primary schools and child health services as large cohorts grow.
choices.D: The working-age population would expand immediately, without a lag as the large child cohorts mature.

questions.note: A youthful age structure tends to increase demand for schools, child health, and later employment as cohorts age.

questions.question: A new highway cuts travel time to a forest frontier. Several years later, clearing accelerates far beyond the road corridor. Which mechanism best explains the effect?

choices.A: Road effects may be strongest near the pavement and remain limited even when access to markets improves.
choices.B: Better access lowers transport costs and can make logging, farming, and settlement more profitable.
choices.C: The road changed local rainfall patterns before improving access to markets or logging areas.
choices.D: The clearing is better explained by natural forest succession than by changes in travel time and access.

questions.note: Infrastructure can induce land-use change by reducing transport costs and opening previously remote areas to economic activity.

questions.question: A map uses a conformal projection that preserves local angles but enlarges Greenland relative to Africa. What should a student avoid using this map to compare?

choices.A: The direction of a short route across a small region.
choices.B: The relative land area of countries and continents.
choices.C: The rough local shape of a coastline at a large scale.
choices.D: Approximate compass bearings over a limited area.

questions.note: Conformal projections preserve angles locally but distort area, often strongly at high latitudes.

questions.question: A dry region receives much of its river water from mountains where glaciers are shrinking. Why might water shortages worsen even before the glaciers disappear?

choices.A: Shrinking ice storage can shift meltwater timing and reduce later dry-season supply.
choices.B: Retreat affects annual water volume but has little influence on seasonal flow.
choices.C: Greater melt can raise runoff while the glaciers remain large, so supply should continue to rise as ice shrinks.
choices.D: Glacier retreat mainly affects settlements located directly on the ice.

questions.note: Glaciers act as seasonal storage; retreat can change the timing and reliability of runoff for distant users.

questions.question: A country reports high annual rainfall, yet many households face dry-season shortages. Which data would most improve a water-security assessment?

choices.A: Monthly rainfall, storage, withdrawals, water quality, and distribution networks.
choices.B: Annual rainfall and reservoir capacity, without withdrawal or quality data.
choices.C: River length and count, without flow, quality, or network coverage.
choices.D: Population and household demand, without regional or seasonal supply data.

questions.note: Water security depends on seasonality, storage, demand, quality, and the ability to deliver usable water.

questions.question: An informal settlement grows on a floodplain despite repeated flood damage. Residents know the risk but cite nearby work and a lack of affordable housing outside the floodplain. Which explanation best fits this evidence?

choices.A: Residents may choose flood-prone land because they believe it has lower exposure than nearby areas.
choices.B: Residents may trade lower housing costs and access to jobs against limited safer options.
choices.C: Residents may expect effective flood protection even where the settlement has weak warnings and infrastructure.
choices.D: Residents often lack any awareness that floods can damage homes and livelihoods.

questions.note: Knowledge of the hazard is stated in the prompt, while limited safe housing and access to jobs explain why exposure can persist.

questions.question: A warm current flows near a coast with moist onshore winds. Farther inland, a mountain range blocks those winds. Which combination best explains wetter coastal slopes and a drier interior?

choices.A: Moist air loses much of its water offshore, then becomes wetter as it descends beyond the mountains.
choices.B: A warm current reduces coastal moisture, while the inland range draws additional water vapor from the air.
choices.C: The mountain range forces descending air upward on its leeward slope, increasing rainfall inland.
choices.D: Moist onshore air rises over windward slopes, while the warm current supplies moisture before a rain shadow forms.

questions.note: Ocean-atmosphere interactions affect moisture, and mountains force uplift on windward slopes while often leaving the lee drier.

questions.question: A country receives 900,000 migrants and has 850,000 emigrants in one year, for net migration of +50,000. What important feature is hidden by the net figure alone?

choices.A: It shows that the country’s total population rose by 50,000 after births and deaths are included.
choices.B: It shows that fewer than 50,000 people changed residence because arrivals and departures largely canceled.
choices.C: It shows that arrivals and departures had similar ages and skills because their totals were close.
choices.D: The net total hides the much larger gross flows and their possible regional effects.

questions.note: Net migration is the balance of arrivals and departures; it hides the scale, direction, and composition of gross flows.

questions.question: After upstream forest removal, a downstream town records faster rises in river level during storms. Which mechanism best connects the land-use change to the flood pattern?

choices.A: Less interception and infiltration can send a larger share of rainfall into streams quickly.
choices.B: Flood peaks are mainly determined by rainfall inside the town, so upstream vegetation is a minor factor.
choices.C: Forest removal affects sediment and water quality but generally leaves the timing of runoff unchanged.
choices.D: Trees mainly affect annual water storage, while storm runoff is controlled by the river channel alone.

questions.note: Removing vegetation and disturbing soils can speed runoff and increase peak flow, though the effect depends on local conditions.

questions.question: A region expands irrigated farming and increases harvests for five years, while groundwater levels fall each year. Which test best determines whether the expansion is sustainable?

choices.A: Compare the latest harvest with the region’s best pre-irrigation harvest and treat growth as the primary sustainability measure.
choices.B: Falling groundwater can be ignored while yields rise, because aquifers commonly recover after irrigation expands.
choices.C: Compare pumping and recharge over time, while examining crop demand and alternatives.
choices.D: Count the number of operating wells and assume more wells indicate a stable supply.

questions.note: A sustainable assessment compares extraction with replenishment and considers whether demand can persist without depleting the aquifer.

questions.question: A river crosses several countries. During drought, an upstream state expands reservoirs while downstream farms face shortages. Which factor most directly shapes whether this becomes a political crisis?

choices.A: Reservoir capacity alone determines downstream security, independent of agreements.
choices.B: Allocation rules, agreements, seasonality, and bargaining power shape whether drought becomes a crisis.
choices.C: Average annual discharge is enough to settle disputes without examining allocation rules.
choices.D: A country’s annual rainfall determines its fair share regardless of storage and timing.

questions.note: Transboundary water stress becomes political through allocation rules, institutions, bargaining power, and perceived fairness.

questions.question: A city plants trees and builds cooling centers in wealthy districts, while low-income districts remain hotter and lose tenants as rents rise near new parks. Which policy package best addresses both heat risk and uneven benefits?

choices.A: Target cooling with heat and vulnerability data, protect tenants, and monitor displacement.
choices.B: Expand trees where land is easiest to acquire, then rely on citywide averages to judge outcomes.
choices.C: Use a uniform planting target in each district and compare total canopy growth.
choices.D: Prioritize cooling and tax-base gains, then review access and displacement after construction.

questions.note: Climate adaptation should reduce exposure while tracking who benefits and preventing improvements from displacing vulnerable residents.

questions.question: A landslide-hazard map ranks locations only by slope steepness. After heavy rain, failures cluster on cut slopes with weak soil. What is the map’s principal flaw?

choices.A: A more precise slope measurement can capture most other causes of slope failure.
choices.B: Slope alone omits rainfall, geology, soil strength, vegetation, and human modification.
choices.C: The map accounts for rainfall but not the way cuts alter local slope stability.
choices.D: The map confuses hazard with risk by leaving out population and assets at risk.

questions.note: Because the map is intended to estimate landslide hazard, it must account for conditions such as rainfall, geology, soil strength, vegetation, and human modification—not just slope angle.

questions.question: Two districts face the same cyclone wind speeds. One has sturdy housing, reliable warnings, and evacuation routes; the other does not. Why may national hazard averages mislead planners?

choices.A: Equal peak wind speeds usually imply similar losses after adjusting for population, even where evacuation access differs.
choices.B: Housing quality and evacuation routes mainly change property damage, with little effect on risk to life.
choices.C: National averages are useful for broad planning, but local preparedness rarely changes the impact of the same hazard.
choices.D: Exposure and capacity to prepare, evacuate, and recover vary locally.

questions.note: Disaster risk depends on hazard as well as exposure, vulnerability, infrastructure, and response capacity.

questions.question: A coastal city uses desalination to reduce dependence on rainfall. Which assessment best captures the trade-off?

choices.A: Energy demand, brine, cost, and intake impacts must be weighed against supply reliability.
choices.B: Because desalination supplies water independent of rainfall, the city can focus on plant output while treating energy and brine as secondary operating details.
choices.C: A desalination plant’s energy demand is mostly limited to construction, so operating costs tend to be minor.
choices.D: Because brine comes from seawater, discharging it has little effect on nearby ecosystems.

questions.note: Desalination can diversify supply but requires energy and creates concentrated brine; costs and local impacts matter.

questions.question: A country has abundant river water, but remote households receive unsafe water intermittently. Which diagnosis best explains the gap?

choices.A: Treatment, infrastructure, distance, seasonal variation, and distribution determine usable access.
choices.B: Abundant raw water usually ensures household access, so the gap mainly reflects differences in household demand.
choices.C: Intermittent supply usually indicates too little annual water volume rather than treatment or distribution failures.
choices.D: Remote households can draw on nearby rivers, making water treatment and distribution networks less important.

questions.note: Physical abundance is not the same as accessible, safe, and reliable household supply.

questions.question: Using the same map projection, shoreline definition, and tide reference, a coastline measured from a coarse map is shorter than one measured using much finer detail. Which explanation is most appropriate?

choices.A: Coarse maps average out small bends, but map scale does not materially affect measured shoreline length.
choices.B: Even with the same projection, the coastline length changes mainly because map scale shifts the distance between endpoints.
choices.C: The discrepancy mainly reflects changing tides and shoreline definitions, not the level of measurement detail.
choices.D: Fine measurements capture more small bends and inlets, increasing measured length

questions.note: When projection, shoreline definition, and tide reference are held constant, finer measurement captures more small-scale irregularity. This is the coastline paradox.

questions.question: A landlocked state sends most trade through one neighboring country’s rail network. A diplomatic dispute closes the border. What vulnerability has been exposed?

choices.A: A single route can make customs simpler, so dependence on the transit state is generally reduced.
choices.B: Concentrating transit through one state creates a chokepoint that can disrupt trade.
choices.C: The closure exposes a chokepoint, but landlocked states can normally switch to sea transport without major new routes.
choices.D: The principal vulnerability is port ownership; a transit state usually cannot interrupt trade carried on its rail network.

questions.note: Dependence on a single corridor creates exposure to border closures, transit fees, and diplomatic disputes.

questions.question: A country has moderate national population density, but two cities suffer severe congestion and housing pressure. Which planning conclusion follows?

choices.A: Moderate national density makes congestion more likely to come from temporary tourism than from urban concentration.
choices.B: National averages are generally reliable for housing and transport planning because dense districts balance out rural space.
choices.C: National average density can hide intense urban concentration and unmet infrastructure demand.
choices.D: Similar national densities call for similar infrastructure in rural areas and large metropolitan centers.

questions.note: National averages can mask dense urban clusters and spatial mismatches between people, jobs, housing, and infrastructure.

questions.question: A student doubles the mass of a cart while keeping its net force constant. According to Newton's second law, what happens to its acceleration?

choices.A: It is halved
choices.B: It stays the same
choices.C: It becomes zero
choices.D: It doubles

questions.note: Since a = F/m, doubling mass at constant net force halves acceleration.

questions.question: Which part of an animal cell holds most of its DNA?

choices.A: Cytoplasm
choices.B: Cell membrane
choices.C: Nucleus
choices.D: Ribosome

questions.note: Ribosomes build proteins; the membrane encloses the cell.

questions.question: Which force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?

choices.A: Magnetism
choices.B: Gravity
choices.C: Friction
choices.D: Inertia

questions.note: Inertia alone would send planets off in straight lines.

questions.question: At sea level, water boils at what temperature?
questions.note: Equal to 212 °F.

questions.question: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?

choices.A: Saturn
choices.B: Neptune
choices.C: Uranus
choices.D: Jupiter

questions.note: Jupiter is over 300 times Earth's mass.

questions.question: What is the hardest natural substance?

choices.A: Quartz
choices.B: Granite
choices.C: Topaz
choices.D: Diamond

questions.note: Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale.

questions.question: What kind of animal is a whale?

choices.A: Reptile
choices.B: Mammal
choices.C: Fish
choices.D: Amphibian

questions.note: Whales breathe air and nurse their young.

questions.question: Scientific knowledge check: What is the chemical formula for water?

choices.A: H₂O
choices.B: H₂O₂
choices.C: O₂
choices.D: CO₂

questions.note: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide.

questions.question: Which gas do plants take in for photosynthesis?

choices.A: Carbon dioxide
choices.B: Carbon monoxide
choices.C: Oxygen
choices.D: Nitrogen

questions.note: Plants release oxygen as a by-product.

questions.question: Which organ produces insulin?

choices.A: Liver
choices.B: Pancreas
choices.C: Gallbladder
choices.D: Kidney

questions.note: Insulin comes from beta cells in the pancreas.

questions.question: A 12 V battery is connected across a 6 Ω resistor. What current flows through the resistor?

choices.A: 6 A
choices.B: 2 A

questions.note: Ohm's law gives I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Na?

choices.A: Magnesium
choices.B: Nickel
choices.C: Sodium
choices.D: Neon

questions.note: Na is the symbol for sodium; neon is Ne, nickel is Ni, and magnesium is Mg.

questions.question: Through which material does sound travel fastest?

choices.A: Water
choices.B: Air
choices.C: Wood
choices.D: Steel

questions.note: Sound is fastest in solids and cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.question: Which subatomic particle has a negative charge?

choices.A: Electron
choices.B: Neutron
choices.C: Positron
choices.D: Proton

questions.note: Protons and positrons are positive; neutrons are neutral.

questions.question: Which type of rock forms when magma cools?

choices.A: Sedimentary
choices.B: Clastic
choices.C: Metamorphic
choices.D: Igneous

questions.note: Clastic rocks are a kind of sedimentary rock.

questions.question: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.note: Neutral is pH 7.

questions.question: A person sees a lightning flash and hears thunder several seconds later. What best explains the delay?

choices.A: Thunder is produced when rain reaches the ground
choices.B: Sound from the discharge travels much more slowly than light
choices.C: Clouds delay the sound by storing it until the flash ends
choices.D: Thunder is produced several seconds after the lightning flash, rather than during the same discharge.

questions.note: The flash and thunder are produced at nearly the same time, but light reaches the observer much faster than sound.

questions.question: Which gas forms when baking soda reacts with vinegar?

choices.A: Carbon dioxide
choices.B: Hydrogen
choices.C: Carbon monoxide
choices.D: Oxygen

questions.note: An acid–base reaction releases CO₂ bubbles.

questions.question: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?

choices.A: Veins
choices.B: Arteries
choices.C: Capillaries
choices.D: Venules

questions.note: Veins return blood to the heart.

questions.question: Which element has atomic number 6?

choices.A: Boron
choices.B: Nitrogen
choices.C: Carbon
choices.D: Oxygen

questions.note: Boron is 5, nitrogen 7, oxygen 8.

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward. At the instant it changes direction, air resistance is negligible. Which statement describes the ball?

choices.A: Its velocity is upward at the top, while gravitational acceleration briefly becomes zero.
choices.B: Its velocity is momentarily zero, but gravitational acceleration still points downward.
choices.C: Both velocity and gravitational acceleration are zero at the instant of reversal.
choices.D: Gravity stops acting at the top and begins again as the ball falls.

questions.note: At the highest point the vertical velocity is momentarily zero, but gravitational acceleration remains downward throughout the flight.

questions.question: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction that has already reached equilibrium. What happens after the catalyst is added, assuming temperature stays constant?

choices.A: The reaction becomes irreversible as activation energy falls
choices.B: More products remain permanently because the reverse reaction stops
choices.C: Both forward and reverse rates rise, reaching equilibrium sooner without changing K.
choices.D: The equilibrium constant increases because the forward reaction speeds up

questions.note: A catalyst lowers activation barriers for both directions; at a fixed temperature it changes the rate of reaching equilibrium, not the equilibrium constant.

questions.question: A weather balloon measures ozone concentration peaking roughly 20–30 km above Earth. Which layer contains most of this protective ozone?

choices.A: The mesosphere
choices.B: The stratosphere
choices.C: The troposphere
choices.D: The thermosphere

questions.note: Most atmospheric ozone is in the stratosphere, where it absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation.

questions.question: A sealed container of gas is heated while its volume stays constant. Assuming the gas amount does not change, what happens to its pressure?

choices.A: It falls because faster molecules collide with the container walls less often.
choices.B: It remains constant because the container’s volume cannot expand.
choices.C: It falls because the gas particles move farther apart as temperature rises.
choices.D: It rises because the warmer gas particles collide with the walls more frequently and forcefully.

questions.note: At constant volume and fixed gas amount, heating raises the gas pressure because particle kinetic energy increases.

questions.question: Two strands of DNA pair through complementary bases. Which pairing pattern helps one strand specify the sequence of the other?

choices.A: A pairs with G, while C pairs with T.
choices.B: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.
choices.C: A pairs with T, while C can pair with either G or A depending on the strand.
choices.D: A pairs with U in DNA, while C pairs with G.

questions.note: In standard DNA base pairing, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine.

questions.question: An unknown gas is colorless, exists as single atoms, and is very unreactive under ordinary conditions. Which periodic-table family is the best place to look first?

choices.A: The noble gases
choices.B: The alkaline-earth metals
choices.C: The alkali metals
choices.D: The halogens

questions.note: Noble gases are generally monatomic and unreactive because their outer electron shells are filled.

questions.question: A bowling ball and tennis ball are released from the same height at the same time in a vacuum. Which prediction follows from the ideal model?

choices.A: The bowling ball reaches the ground first because its weight is greater
choices.B: The tennis ball reaches the ground first because it is easier to accelerate
choices.C: They have the same downward acceleration and land together
choices.D: Their landing times depend on their masses but not their shapes

questions.note: In a vacuum, objects near Earth fall with the same gravitational acceleration regardless of mass.

questions.question: An ice cube floats in a glass of liquid water. Which microscopic change best explains this observation?

choices.A: Water molecules pack more tightly into ice than into liquid water
choices.B: Ice is held at the surface mainly by surface tension
choices.C: Liquid water becomes denser as it freezes
choices.D: Freezing creates a structure that spaces water molecules farther apart

questions.note: The open crystal structure of ordinary ice makes it less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

questions.question: Sunlight contains many visible wavelengths, yet a clear daytime sky looks blue from the ground. Which process best explains this?

choices.A: Air molecules scatter shorter visible wavelengths more strongly than longer ones.
choices.B: Ozone emits blue light after absorbing sunlight in the upper atmosphere.
choices.C: The blue appearance mainly comes from reflection off the ocean surface rather than atmospheric scattering.
choices.D: Air molecules scatter longer visible wavelengths more strongly than shorter ones.

questions.note: Rayleigh scattering by molecules in the atmosphere is stronger at shorter visible wavelengths, making the sky appear blue.

questions.question: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same room overnight. The metal feels colder when touched. What best explains the sensation?

choices.A: Metal feels colder because it transfers heat away from skin faster than many other materials.
choices.B: Metal feels colder because it begins at a lower temperature than wood, even after both have equilibrated in the same room.
choices.C: Metal feels colder mainly because its density is greater, regardless of thermal conductivity.
choices.D: Metal usually reaches a lower equilibrium temperature than wood when both are left indoors overnight.

questions.note: At the same temperature, metal typically draws heat from the skin faster because its thermal conductivity is higher.

questions.question: In an undisturbed rock sequence, layer A lies below layer B. A volcanic dike cuts through both layers but does not cut a younger layer C above them. Which event is youngest among A, B, the dike, and C?

choices.A: Layer B was deposited
choices.B: Layer C was deposited
choices.C: Layer A was deposited
choices.D: The dike intruded through A and B

questions.note: Superposition makes A older than B; cross-cutting makes the dike younger than A and B, while C was deposited after the dike because the dike does not cut it.

questions.question: A disease spreads through a small population that has very little genetic variation. Why might the population be less resilient?

choices.A: Low genetic variation affects long-term adaptation but has little bearing on how a population responds to a current outbreak.
choices.B: Limited variation may leave fewer individuals carrying traits that reduce susceptibility.
choices.C: A genetically uniform population is less likely to encounter pathogens because individuals share similar traits.
choices.D: Genetic diversity mostly changes visible characteristics; disease resistance usually varies independently of it.

questions.note: Genetic variation does not guarantee resistance, but it can increase the chance that some individuals have traits that help them survive a new threat.

questions.question: Two 6 Ω resistors are connected in parallel to an ideal battery. Compared with one 6 Ω resistor alone, what happens to the equivalent resistance and total current from the battery?

choices.A: Resistance doubles and current halves
choices.B: Resistance falls to 1.5 Ω and total current quadruples
choices.C: Resistance stays at 6 Ω and current stays unchanged
choices.D: Resistance falls to 3 Ω and total current doubles

questions.note: For two equal resistors in parallel, R_eq = 3 Ω; at fixed voltage, halving resistance doubles total current.

questions.question: An astronaut in orbit stands on a scale inside a spacecraft. The spacecraft’s engines are off and it is in free fall around Earth. What scale reading is expected, and why?

choices.A: Nearly zero, because the spacecraft is outside the region where Earth’s gravity has a meaningful effect.
choices.B: Greater than normal, because orbital speed adds directly to the astronaut’s weight on the scale.
choices.C: Nearly zero, because astronaut and spacecraft accelerate together under gravity
choices.D: Near the surface-weight reading, because the astronaut still experiences most of Earth’s gravitational pull.

questions.note: Apparent weight depends on contact force. In orbital free fall, the astronaut and scale accelerate together, producing a near-zero reading despite substantial gravity.

questions.question: Two parents are both Bb, with B dominant over b. Assuming independent inheritance for each child, what is the probability that exactly one of their next two children is bb?
questions.note: Each child has a 1/4 chance of bb and a 3/4 chance of not bb. Exactly one affected child has probability 2 × (1/4)(3/4) = 3/8.

questions.question: A patient has a viral infection and takes antibiotics unnecessarily. Which consequence is most scientifically supported?

choices.A: The drug does not treat the virus but can select for resistant bacteria.
choices.B: Antibiotics prevent the immune system from recognizing viruses.
choices.C: Antibiotics eliminate the virus directly because it reproduces inside cells.
choices.D: A single unnecessary course makes most bacteria in the body resistant at once.

questions.note: Antibiotics do not treat viruses, but unnecessary use can favor antibiotic-resistant bacteria through natural selection.

questions.question: A solid weighs 30 N in air and has an apparent weight of 20 N when fully submerged in water. Assume buoyancy is due to displaced water. What is the solid’s average density relative to water?

choices.A: 2 times water’s density
choices.B: 1.5 times water’s density
choices.C: 3 times water’s density
choices.D: 0.5 times water’s density

questions.note: The buoyant force is 10 N, equal to the weight of displaced water; the solid’s weight is 30 N, so its density is three times water’s.

questions.question: A beam of light enters water from air at an angle. Its frequency remains the same, while its speed decreases. What happens to its wavelength?

choices.A: It decreases because wavelength equals speed divided by frequency.
choices.B: It remains unchanged because the frequency is conserved at the boundary.
choices.C: It increases because bending toward the normal stretches the wave between crests.
choices.D: It decreases because both speed and frequency fall in the same proportion.

questions.note: Frequency is set by the source and remains constant across the boundary; lower speed therefore means shorter wavelength in water.

questions.question: A car moves around a circular track at constant speed. Which observation confirms that it accelerates?

choices.A: Its velocity direction changes even though its speed remains constant.
choices.B: Its kinetic energy rises because the car travels a longer distance during each turn.
choices.C: Its net force is zero because a constant speed means its velocity is constant.
choices.D: Its acceleration is zero unless the car changes both speed and direction.

questions.note: Velocity includes direction, so changing direction means acceleration; circular motion requires inward net force.

questions.question: On a sunny day, the ground warms strongly while air temperature usually falls with increasing altitude through much of the troposphere. Which explanation best accounts for this?

choices.A: High-altitude air is colder mainly because it is much farther from the Sun.
choices.B: Gravity cools rising air by removing thermal energy, independent of changes in pressure.
choices.C: Clouds absorb most solar energy and then warm the ground from above.
choices.D: The ground warms lower air, while rising air expands and cools as pressure falls.

questions.note: The surface absorbs solar energy and warms nearby air; rising air expands in lower pressure and cools, although weather and inversions can change the local profile.

questions.question: A clinical trial reports that a new drug reduces symptoms, but the treatment group is younger on average than the control group. Which analysis is most appropriate?

choices.A: A difference in average age is harmless once treatment was assigned randomly, even if the trial was small.
choices.B: Check whether age affects outcomes and adjust the design or analysis for the imbalance.
choices.C: Improvement from baseline proves effectiveness as long as symptoms declined after the drug was given.
choices.D: Age matters only when it was named as a planned outcome before the trial began.

questions.note: If age is related to outcomes, uneven age distribution can confound the observed treatment difference; randomization or adjustment helps address this.

questions.question: A population initially grows rapidly, then its growth rate slows as food and space become limiting. Which model best represents this pattern?

choices.A: Logistic growth approaching a carrying capacity
choices.B: Unrestricted exponential growth at an unchanged per-capita rate
choices.C: Linear growth at a fixed number of individuals per year
choices.D: Radioactive decay with a constant half-life

questions.note: Logistic growth incorporates density-dependent limits and slows as population size approaches carrying capacity.

questions.question: Two treatments have similar average symptom reduction in a study. What further evidence is most important before treating them as clinically interchangeable?

choices.A: Whether the average benefit is statistically significant in each study, without comparing harms or the patients enrolled.
choices.B: Differences in adverse effects, interactions, duration, patient subgroups, and evidence quality
choices.C: Whether the studies used the same follow-up schedule and reported effects to the same number of decimal places.
choices.D: Whether the treatments produced similar averages in the full samples, regardless of uncertainty or subgroup effects.

questions.note: Comparable average efficacy does not establish equal safety or suitability across different patients and settings.

questions.question: A solution changes from pH 3 to pH 5. Assuming the pH values are accurate, how does hydrogen-ion concentration change?

choices.A: It decreases by a factor of 2
choices.B: It decreases by a factor of 10
choices.C: It decreases by a factor of 100
choices.D: It increases by a factor of 100

questions.note: Each whole-number increase in pH represents a tenfold decrease in hydrogen-ion concentration; two pH units mean a hundredfold decrease.

questions.question: A species survives one extreme heatwave, but heatwaves recur every year before its population fully recovers. Why can the long-term trend still be negative?

choices.A: Population recovery depends mainly on adult counts; changes in reproduction matter only after numbers have fallen sharply.
choices.B: Survival through one heatwave indicates the species is adapted to the conditions, even if extreme events recur.
choices.C: If adult survival stays high, repeated heatwaves should not affect long-term growth even when breeding seasons are disrupted.
choices.D: Repeated stress can reduce reproduction and survival before the population fully recovers.

questions.note: Repeated disturbances can reduce reproductive success and recovery, even if one event does not immediately cause a population collapse.

questions.question: A satellite has enough tangential speed to remain in a stable circular orbit. Which description best explains its motion?

choices.A: Gravity continually bends the path toward Earth while sideways velocity carries the satellite forward.
choices.B: Its inertia cancels gravity exactly, leaving the satellite to follow a straight path around Earth.
choices.C: Gravity becomes negligible above the atmosphere, so the satellite can orbit without a central force.
choices.D: An outward force balances gravity, leaving the satellite with no acceleration toward Earth.

questions.note: An orbit is continuous free fall; gravity provides the inward acceleration while tangential velocity prevents a direct fall to the surface.

questions.question: A study finds that teenagers with more screen time report poorer sleep. Which follow-up would best strengthen a causal interpretation?

choices.A: Measure key confounders and, where feasible, test a controlled reduction in evening screen use.
choices.B: Repeat the same survey with more participants; a larger sample alone can distinguish causal effects from confounding.
choices.C: Measure screen time and sleep more precisely, but avoid measuring schedules or stress because they may complicate the analysis.
choices.D: Recruit people with poor sleep first and use their recalled screen time to estimate what caused the sleep difference.

questions.note: Confounders and reverse causation are possible; a controlled intervention or carefully designed longitudinal study can improve causal inference.

questions.question: A plant has adequate water and light but receives very little carbon dioxide. Which stage of photosynthesis is most directly limited first by the shortage?

choices.A: Absorption of photons by chlorophyll
choices.B: Splitting of water by light in the thylakoid membrane
choices.C: Carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle
choices.D: Movement of existing sugars through the phloem

questions.note: Carbon dioxide is a substrate for carbon fixation; adequate light and water do not remove that limitation.

questions.question: A cell’s nucleus is damaged, but its cytoplasm and mitochondria remain functional briefly. Which prediction best describes a likely longer-term consequence?

choices.A: Existing cytoplasmic enzymes become inactive immediately, before nuclear gene expression changes.
choices.B: Translation stops throughout the cell because functional ribosomes are stored inside the nucleus.
choices.C: Nuclear damage changes cell shape, but transcription and production of new RNAs continue normally.
choices.D: Transcriptional control is impaired, limiting renewal of many RNAs and proteins while existing activity may persist.

questions.note: The nucleus contains most DNA and is central to transcription; existing RNAs, proteins, and mitochondrial activity can persist temporarily.

questions.question: A patient has a normal red-blood-cell count but low hemoglobin concentration. Which effect is most directly expected?

choices.A: The blood may clot more slowly because hemoglobin is the protein that activates platelets.
choices.B: Oxygen-carrying capacity can be reduced despite a normal red-cell count.
choices.C: Oxygen delivery should remain normal because red-cell count alone determines oxygen-carrying capacity.
choices.D: The immune response may weaken because hemoglobin is required to make antibodies.

questions.note: Hemoglobin carries oxygen; a normal number of red cells does not guarantee normal oxygen capacity if each contains less hemoglobin.

questions.question: A researcher tests 20 unrelated hypotheses and reports only the two with p-values below 0.05. What is the central statistical concern?

choices.A: The false-positive risk depends on effect size, not on how many hypotheses were tested.
choices.B: A p-value below 0.05 means the hypothesis has about a 95% chance of being true.
choices.C: Multiple testing and selective reporting can make chance findings appear unusually convincing.
choices.D: Independent tests remove the need to account for how many hypotheses are reported.

questions.note: When many hypotheses are tested, some may meet the threshold by chance; selective reporting further exaggerates apparent evidence.

questions.question: A species survives in a wide range of temperatures in laboratory conditions but occupies only a narrow range in nature. Which explanation best distinguishes its fundamental and realized niches?

choices.A: The fundamental niche includes competitors and predators as defining limits by itself.
choices.B: The realized niche is the full range the species could occupy without competitors.
choices.C: The gap between lab and nature is most likely a temperature-sensor error.
choices.D: Competitors and other conditions can narrow the realized niche within the fundamental niche.

questions.note: The fundamental niche describes abiotic conditions the species can tolerate; biotic interactions and other constraints can narrow the realized niche.

questions.question: A climate model fits past temperature data extremely well but performs poorly on data collected later. Which evaluation is most useful?

choices.A: The new data should be discounted until they match the model’s original calibration period.
choices.B: Poor later performance proves that historical observations were unsuitable for evaluating the model.
choices.C: Check for overfitting, missing processes, and whether later data differ from calibration conditions.
choices.D: Add parameters until the model reproduces the calibration data more closely, even if the later data remain unexplained.

questions.note: A good fit to training data is not sufficient; out-of-sample performance helps reveal overfitting and structural problems.

questions.question: Two individuals carry the same gene variant, but its effect differs between them because they have different genetic backgrounds and environments. Which principle best explains this?

choices.A: Gene effects can depend on interactions with other genes and environmental conditions.
choices.B: The same variant usually produces the same trait regardless of genetic background or environment.
choices.C: Environmental changes can alter gene expression but rarely influence observable traits.
choices.D: Dominance is the main factor in a variant’s effect, with other genes playing a limited role.

questions.note: Phenotypes emerge from interactions among variants, genetic background, development, and environment.

questions.question: A restored wetland has more species than before, but most of the increase comes from a few invasive generalists while specialist species decline. What is the best evaluation?

choices.A: The total count hides changes in composition and abundance, so success depends on restoration goals.
choices.B: More generalist species can compensate for specialist losses under most conservation goals.
choices.C: A rise in total species count is strong evidence that ecosystem function has recovered.
choices.D: Species richness can be a useful measure even when the identity of added species is not considered.

questions.note: Richness alone can hide losses of native specialists or changes in abundance; indicators should match the ecological objective.

questions.question: An observational study finds that people who take a supplement have lower disease rates. Which concern most limits a causal conclusion?

choices.A: Randomized trials mainly establish causation when participants can identify their assigned treatment.
choices.B: Supplement users may differ in health, income, behavior, or access to care.
choices.C: Observational studies provide no useful information about associations between variables.
choices.D: A large sample usually makes confounding negligible because individual differences average out.

questions.note: Confounding and selection effects can explain associations in observational data; design and analysis must address alternative explanations.

questions.question: An atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. It gains one electron and becomes an ion. Which description is correct?

choices.A: Atomic number 17, mass number 35, charge +1
choices.B: Atomic number 17, mass number 35, charge −1
choices.C: Atomic number 18, mass number 35, charge −1
choices.D: Atomic number 17, mass number 36, charge −1

questions.note: Atomic number equals protons (17); mass number is protons plus neutrons (35); one extra electron gives a −1 charge. The distractors reflect confusion between charge, atomic number, and mass number.

questions.question: An igneous rock contains large crystals surrounded by much finer crystals. What cooling history is the best explanation?

choices.A: Large and small crystals grew together at the same rate deep underground.
choices.B: Some crystals grew slowly before the remaining melt cooled more quickly.
choices.C: The large crystals formed during rapid surface cooling, while the small crystals developed first at depth.
choices.D: The large crystals are older sediment grains, and the smaller crystals formed as cement during burial.

questions.note: A porphyritic texture commonly records at least two stages of cooling, with larger crystals forming before the finer groundmass.

questions.question: A lightning flash and its thunder are produced at essentially the same time. At distance d, let v_sound and v_light be the speeds of sound and light. Which expression gives the exact arrival-time delay of thunder relative to the flash?

choices.A: d ÷ v_sound − d ÷ v_light
choices.B: d ÷ v_light − d ÷ v_sound
choices.C: d ÷ (v_sound + v_light)
choices.D: d ÷ v_sound + d ÷ v_light

questions.note: The delay equals the sound travel time minus the light travel time: d/v_sound − d/v_light. Light travel time is tiny at everyday distances, but the expression includes both travel times.

questions.question: A 0.50 kg object is launched vertically by a spring with 4.0 J of stored elastic energy. If 1.0 J is lost to heat and sound and air resistance is negligible, what maximum height above the release point can it reach? Use g = 10 m/s².
questions.note: The energy available for gravitational potential energy is 4.0−1.0=3.0 J. Set mgh=3.0 J: h=3.0/(0.50×10)=0.60 m. The distractors reflect forgetting the losses or using the wrong mass/energy relationship.

questions.question: A jacket costs $80 and is discounted by 25%. What is the sale price?

questions.question: A bag contains 5 red and 7 blue tokens. Two tokens are drawn without replacement. What is the probability of getting exactly one red token?
questions.note: There are two orders: red then blue or blue then red. The probability is (5/12)(7/11) + (7/12)(5/11) = 35/66.

questions.question: A price is reduced by 20%, then the reduced price is lowered by another 10%. What is the total percentage decrease from the original price?
questions.note: After the changes, 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72 of the original remains, so the total decrease is 28%.

questions.question: Two warning lights flash every 14 minutes and every 20 minutes. They flash together at 9:00 a.m. When will they next flash together?
questions.note: They coincide every least common multiple of 14 and 20 minutes: LCM = 140 minutes, which is 2 hours 20 minutes after 9:00.

questions.question: Solve the equation (2x − 3)/5 = (x + 4)/3.
questions.note: Cross-multiply: 3(2x−3)=5(x+4), so 6x−9=5x+20 and x=29.

questions.question: Store A sells 8 notebooks for ₱280. Store B sells 5 notebooks for ₱190. How much cheaper per notebook is the better deal?

choices.A: They cost the same
choices.B: Store A by ₱3
choices.C: Store A by ₱1.50
choices.D: Store B by ₱2

questions.note: Store A costs ₱35 each; Store B costs ₱38 each, so Store A is cheaper by ₱3 per notebook.

questions.question: Four friends line up for a photo. Two siblings refuse to stand next to each other. How many different lineups are possible?
questions.note: There are 4! = 24 total lineups. If the siblings stand together, treat them as a block: 3! × 2 = 12. Thus 24−12=12 lineups keep them apart.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that exactly one of them is an ace?
questions.note: There are two orders: ace then non-ace or non-ace then ace. The probability is 2 × (4/52)(48/51) = 32/221.

questions.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 8 hours and Pipe B fills it in 12 hours. A leak empties a full tank in 24 hours. If both pipes and the leak operate together, how long will an empty tank take to fill?

choices.A: 6 hours
choices.B: 8 hours
choices.C: 4 hours
choices.D: 12 hours

questions.note: Net rate = 1/8 + 1/12 − 1/24 = 1/6 tank per hour, so the fill time is 6 hours.

questions.question: Two numbers satisfy x + y = 13 and x − y = 5. What is their product xy?
questions.note: Adding the equations gives 2x=18, so x=9 and y=4; therefore xy=36.

questions.question: A store raises a price by 25% and later discounts the new price by 20%. Compared with the original price, what is the final result?

choices.A: A 10% increase
choices.B: A 5% decrease

choices.D: No change

questions.note: The price is multiplied by 1.25 × 0.80 = 1.00, so it returns to the original amount.

questions.question: A fair six-sided die is rolled twice. What is the probability of getting at least one six?
questions.note: Use the complement: probability of no six is (5/6)² = 25/36, so at least one six has probability 11/36.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have side lengths in the ratio 3:5. If the smaller triangle has area 54 cm², what is the area of the larger triangle?

choices.A: 90 cm²
choices.B: 150 cm²
choices.C: 250 cm²

questions.note: Areas scale by the square of the side ratio: 54 × (5/3)² = 54 × 25/9 = 150 cm².

questions.question: Two positive integers have a sum of 13. What is the greatest product they can have?
questions.note: For a fixed sum, the product is largest when the integers are as close as possible: 6 × 7 = 42.

questions.question: A rectangle has perimeter 42 cm. Its length is 3 cm greater than its width. What is its area?

choices.A: 120 cm²
choices.B: 90 cm²
choices.C: 96 cm²
choices.D: 108 cm²

questions.note: L+W=21 and L=W+3, giving W=9 and L=12; the area is 108 cm².

questions.question: If 2^(x+1) × 4^(x−1) = 128, what is x?
questions.note: Rewrite 4 as 2²: the product is 2^(x+1+2x−2)=2^(3x−1)=2^7, so 3x−1=7 and x=8/3.

questions.question: What is the sum of all integers from 1 through 100 that are not divisible by 3?
questions.note: The sum 1 through 100 is 5050. Multiples of 3 sum to 3(1+…+33)=3×561=1683. Difference: 5050−1683=3367.

questions.question: How many three-digit positive integers have digits that strictly increase from left to right?
questions.note: Choose any 3 distinct digits from 1–9; once chosen, there is exactly one increasing order. Thus the count is C(9,3)=84.

questions.question: A committee of four is chosen from eight people, two of whom are siblings. How many committees contain at least one of the siblings?
questions.note: There are C(8,4)=70 committees total. Committees containing neither sibling are C(6,4)=15, so 70−15=55 contain at least one.

questions.question: How many positive integer divisors does 360 have, including 1 and 360?
questions.note: Prime factorization: 360=2³×3²×5¹. The divisor count is (3+1)(2+1)(1+1)=24.

questions.question: A positive integer leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5 and a remainder of 1 when divided by 3. What is the smallest such integer greater than 20?
questions.note: Numbers that leave remainder 2 upon division by 5 include 22, 27, 32, 37, …; 22 also leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3, and it is the smallest above 20.

questions.question: A quadratic has roots 2 and −5 and passes through the point (0, −30). Which equation matches it?

choices.D: y = x² + 3x − 10

questions.note: The roots give y=a(x−2)(x+5). Since y(0)=−10a=−30, a=3, yielding 3x²+9x−30.

questions.question: An arithmetic sequence has a₃ = 11 and a₈ = 31. What is the sum of its first eight terms?
questions.note: The common difference is (31−11)/5=4; a₁=11−8=3 and a₈=31. The sum is 8(3+31)/2=136.

questions.question: For x > 4, solve log₁₀(x−1) + log₁₀(x−4) = 1.
questions.note: Combine logs: (x−1)(x−4)=10, so x²−5x−6=0 gives x=6 or −1. Only x=6 satisfies x>4.

questions.question: The radius of a circle increases by 20%. By what percentage does its area increase?
questions.note: Area is proportional to r²; the new area factor is 1.2²=1.44, so the increase is 44%.

questions.question: A box has 4 red and 6 blue tokens. Three tokens are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that all three are the same color?

questions.question: The mean of six numbers is 15. When one of the numbers is removed, the mean of the remaining five numbers is 13. What number was removed?

questions.question: A right triangle has legs 9 cm and 12 cm. A circle is inscribed in it. What is the circle’s area?

questions.question: Events A and B are independent with P(A)=0.4 and P(B)=0.5. Given that at least one occurs, what is the probability that both occur?

questions.question: A quadratic polynomial p(x)=x²+ax+b leaves remainder 4 when divided by x−2 and remainder −1 when divided by x+1. What is a+b?

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed until the first head. What is the probability the first head appears on an even-numbered toss?
questions.note: The probability is 1/4+1/16+1/64+…; this geometric series has sum (1/4)/(1−1/4)=1/3.

questions.question: Positive numbers a and b satisfy a+b=10. What is the maximum value of a²b?

questions.question: A geometric sequence has first term 3 and common ratio 2. What is the smallest n for which the sum of its first n terms exceeds 1,000?

questions.question: Two positive numbers x and y have sum 12. What is the minimum value of x² + 2y²?

questions.question: A continuous random variable has probability density f(x)=kx on 0≤x≤2 and zero elsewhere. What is P(1≤X≤2)?

questions.question: A data set has mean 18. After a new value of 30 is added, the mean rises to 19. How many values were in the original data set?

questions.question: A car must cover 180 km in 2 hours 15 minutes. It travels the first 60 km at 40 km/h. What average speed must it maintain over the remaining 120 km to finish on time?

questions.question: A crew of five finishes a job in 12 days at a constant rate. After four days, two workers leave. How many additional days will the remaining three workers need?
