choices.C: It organized the main armed forces that fought Spanish troops
choices.D: It negotiated the terms of independence directly with Spanish officials

questions.note: La Solidaridad was a newspaper associated with the Propaganda Movement.

questions.question: Why is the date a law was passed insufficient for understanding its social impact?

choices.A: The date of a law can matter when historians examine the political context and implementation
choices.B: Its wording and stated purpose establish its outcome without further evidence
choices.C: Enforcement, access, institutions, and the distribution of costs and benefits also matter
choices.D: Once a law takes effect, its social consequences can usually be inferred without studying enforcement or who benefits.

questions.note: A law’s effects depend on implementation and social conditions, not just the formal date of passage.

questions.question: What does the presence of resistance movements in different Philippine regions before 1896 suggest?

choices.A: Local conditions shaped diverse grievances and leaders before a nationwide revolution emerged.
choices.B: A single national command organized resistance movements across the archipelago from their earliest stages.
choices.C: Regional uprisings developed independently and therefore shared few grievances against colonial rule.
choices.D: Movements that opposed Spain necessarily shared the same leaders, goals, and strategy.

questions.note: Regional resistance shows that grievances and leadership developed in different local settings; it does not by itself prove there was already one unified national command or strategy.

questions.question: Why is the Katipunan not interchangeable with the entire Philippine Revolution?

choices.A: The Revolution included people and political goals beyond one organization, and the movement changed over time
choices.B: The Katipunan played little role in initiating armed resistance in 1896.
choices.C: All revolutionary groups followed the Katipunan’s command structure throughout the conflict.
choices.D: The Katipunan organized resistance before independence was recognized in 1946.

questions.note: The Katipunan was important to the outbreak of the Revolution, but the wider struggle involved broader participants, regions, and political projects.

questions.question: What was the historical significance of the Malolos Congress?

choices.A: It formalized independence after the United States recognized the republic
choices.B: It attempted to establish representative constitutional government during wartime
choices.C: It established the Commonwealth government under American rule
choices.D: It served as a legislature within the Spanish colonial administration

questions.note: The Congress attempted to establish a representative constitutional government while the war for independence continued.

questions.question: Why must the Commonwealth government be distinguished from full independence in 1946?

choices.A: The Commonwealth began after the United States recognized independence
choices.B: The 1946 transition changed the government’s name but not its legal status
choices.C: The Commonwealth exercised the same international sovereignty as an independent state
choices.D: The Commonwealth was a transitional government before recognized independence

questions.note: The Commonwealth was a transitional self-governing period before recognized independence in 1946.

questions.question: Why compare accounts from different participants in the 1986 EDSA uprising?

choices.A: Assume eyewitnesses shared the same motives and interpretation.
choices.B: Compare viewpoints, check claims, and note differences.
choices.C: Let the best-known participant define the whole narrative.
choices.D: Replace written records with personal recollections.

questions.note: Different accounts can reveal varied experiences and claims; historians still compare them with independent evidence and context.

questions.question: Philippine history challenge: The Bataan Death March took place during which period?

choices.A: Spanish colonial era
choices.B: Martial law era
choices.C: Philippine–American War
choices.D: Japanese occupation

questions.note: April 1942, after the fall of Bataan.

questions.question: Which action is associated with the Cry of Pugad Lawin in 1896?

choices.A: Signing the Malolos Constitution
choices.B: Agreeing to the Biak-na-Bato pact
choices.C: Tearing cedulas to reject Spanish authority
choices.D: Declaring independence in Kawit

questions.note: The tearing of cédulas became a symbol of rejecting Spanish colonial authority at the beginning of the Revolution.

questions.question: Why did the turn from reform activism toward armed revolution matter to Philippine nationalism in the 1890s?

choices.A: Most reform leaders shared a settled plan for armed resistance even while petitions continued.
choices.B: The shift occurred after Spain had recognized Philippine independence.
choices.C: The turn to armed resistance meant earlier reform activity had no political influence.
choices.D: The shift showed that reform and armed resistance became competing strategies within a changing movement.

questions.note: The shift reflected frustration with reform under colonial rule; reformists and revolutionaries still differed in methods and goals.

questions.question: Two eyewitnesses describe the same uprising differently. One wrote a private letter soon after it; the other gave an official statement under colonial questioning. What should a historian do first?

choices.A: Compare each account’s timing, audience, incentives, wording, and corroborating evidence
choices.B: Treat the accounts as equally accurate and combine their claims without checking them
choices.C: Choose the account with more dramatic details because it is more memorable
choices.D: Accept the official account because the government had access to more records

questions.note: Source criticism compares context, purpose, proximity, and corroboration rather than treating one source type as automatically reliable.

questions.question: The 1898 Treaty of Paris transferred Spain’s claim to the Philippines to the United States. What does that transfer reveal about the treaty’s limits from the Filipino revolutionary government’s perspective?

choices.A: The treaty recognized the revolutionary government as the authority that would decide the islands’ future status.
choices.B: The transfer created an internationally accepted protectorate in which Filipino representatives controlled foreign policy.
choices.C: The two colonial powers negotiated sovereignty without granting the Filipino republic independence
choices.D: Filipino representatives participated in the treaty negotiations and formally consented to the transfer.

questions.note: The treaty transferred Spain’s claim to the United States and did not recognize the First Philippine Republic as an independent state.

questions.question: The Jones Law of 1916 expanded Filipino participation in government but did not immediately end U.S. rule. Which interpretation best captures that combination?

choices.A: The law transferred national sovereignty to the elected Filipino legislature.
choices.B: Filipino participation expanded, while ultimate sovereignty remained under U.S. authority.
choices.C: It removed Filipino participation and replaced elected officials with appointed administrators.
choices.D: It completed the transition to independence while leaving diplomatic recognition outstanding.

questions.note: The Jones Law expanded Filipino control over the legislature and promised eventual independence, but the United States retained sovereignty.

questions.question: How can concentrated landownership affect the relationship between landlords and tenant farmers?

choices.A: It shifts control over local land disputes entirely to tenant organizations
choices.B: It can reduce landlords’ bargaining power by giving tenants more alternatives
choices.C: It can make tenants more dependent on landowners for land and livelihood
choices.D: It tends to remove rent and labor obligations from tenant agreements

questions.note: Concentrated landownership can increase tenants’ dependence on landowners and reinforce unequal bargaining power.

questions.question: During the Philippine Revolution and later conflicts, a military force in one province surrendered while resistance continued elsewhere. Which historical mistake should be avoided?

choices.A: Avoid treating each local force as if it shared identical command, aims, and timing.
choices.B: A surrender in one province is a reliable sign that other provincial commanders had received the same order to stop fighting.
choices.C: The surrender demonstrates that all revolutionary leaders had accepted a single strategy and chain of command.
choices.D: The surrender can establish the precise end date of organized resistance across the archipelago.

questions.note: The archipelago contained different regional forces and conditions; one surrender did not automatically end all resistance.

questions.question: After the Marcos dictatorship, why was restoring constitutional checks in the 1987 Constitution significant?

choices.A: It permanently removed executive authority from the presidency.
choices.B: It rebuilt institutional checks after a period when executive power had been concentrated.
choices.C: It made legislative and judicial checks unnecessary by strengthening the presidency.
choices.D: It restored the exact political institutions that existed before the Commonwealth.

questions.note: The 1987 Constitution restored a bill of rights and mechanisms intended to limit excessive concentration of power.

questions.question: Spanish colonial authorities used reducción to concentrate communities near churches and administrative centers. Which consequence best explains why the policy mattered to colonial rule?

choices.A: It kept communities dispersed, making tribute collection and religious instruction less centralized.
choices.B: It ended local tribute obligations by giving each town control over colonial revenue.
choices.C: It mainly evacuated settlements for military safety and had little effect on daily administration.
choices.D: It concentrated communities where officials could organize administration, tribute collection, and evangelization.

questions.note: Reducción reorganized settlement patterns and made communities more accessible to colonial administration and religious instruction, while reshaping local life.

questions.question: The Tydings–McDuffie Act provided for a transition period before independence. Why did the Commonwealth still not amount to full sovereignty?

choices.A: It created elected Filipino institutions but did not grant immediate national independence.
choices.B: Self-government expanded, but the United States retained key powers during the transition.
choices.C: It returned the islands to direct Spanish rule while postponing a separate transition period.
choices.D: It set a transition period while making independence depend on joining a different commonwealth.

questions.note: The 1935 Commonwealth was a transitional self-governing arrangement; full independence came in 1946, after the interruption of World War II.

questions.question: Opposition to Ferdinand Marcos existed before Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. was assassinated in 1983. Which interpretation best explains why the assassination became a turning point?

choices.A: It became a focal event that linked existing opposition networks and broadened public criticism of the regime.
choices.B: It brought opposition groups into contact but reduced the movement’s ability to mobilize people beyond established political circles.
choices.C: It shifted opposition demands away from political reform and toward a narrow dispute over succession among elites.
choices.D: It redirected opposition strategy mainly toward negotiations abroad, while domestic protest patterns remained largely unchanged.

questions.note: Aquino’s assassination became a focal event for growing opposition; it helped widen public mobilization rather than creating resistance from nothing or immediately ending the regime.

questions.question: The 1898 Declaration of Philippine Independence made a clear claim to sovereignty, but the Treaty of Paris transferred Spain’s claim to the United States. What distinction is essential here?

choices.A: A public declaration establishes international recognition even when other states do not acknowledge it.
choices.B: The Treaty of Paris had been signed before the declaration was made in Kawit.
choices.C: A declaration makes a political claim; recognition and effective control are separate developments.
choices.D: A claim to independence gains legal force only when the former colonial power formally accepts it.

questions.note: A declaration can express sovereignty without securing recognition from other powers or control over the territory.

questions.question: A colonial report and local accounts concern the same province and period. The report labels the province “peaceful,” while local accounts describe forced relocation and resistance. What question should guide the comparison?

choices.A: Do the local accounts use the same administrative boundary and time period as the official report?
choices.B: Which account provides the longest list of incidents, regardless of how each writer gathered information?
choices.C: Was the report produced by a civil office or a military office, independent of what it records?
choices.D: Does the report define peace as absence of open combat while excluding coercion or dissent?

questions.note: Administrative descriptions such as “peaceful” may reflect a government’s criteria rather than the full experience of people in the region.

questions.question: Under Spanish or American rule, a local council may have elected Filipino members while a colonial governor retained veto power. Which conclusion best fits this arrangement?

choices.A: A veto constrained the council only when used, so the possibility of veto power did not shape representation.
choices.B: Local elections could affect representation while a colonial governor retained decisive authority.
choices.C: Local elections transferred external sovereignty to the elected members, even where the governor retained a veto.
choices.D: Local councils had little influence on administration because colonial governors controlled every local decision directly.

questions.note: Colonial institutions could create meaningful local participation without transferring ultimate authority to Filipino officials.

questions.question: Researchers studying Martial Law compare a government memorandum, a survivor’s oral history, and a court record. Why is triangulation stronger than treating one as definitive?

choices.A: Each source has different purposes and limits, so agreement and conflict should be examined together.
choices.B: The oral history should outweigh the other sources because first-person memory is less shaped by institutions.
choices.C: The court record should settle the issue because legal records are more neutral than government memoranda.
choices.D: Triangulation is most useful when sources agree; conflicting evidence can be left aside to avoid bias.

questions.note: Combining sources can reveal corroboration and disagreement while allowing for the distinct limits of each source.

questions.question: How could American colonial administration use local elites without giving them full control over national policy?

choices.A: Local elites could administer communities and build patronage while U.S. authorities retained sovereignty.
choices.B: Local elites were generally barred from civil administration, leaving U.S. officials to govern communities directly.
choices.C: Local elite participation meant that control of foreign affairs and national policy had already shifted to Filipino officials.
choices.D: Local officials could hold ceremonial posts but were excluded from elections and the routine work of administration.

questions.note: Colonial systems can rely on local intermediaries while keeping final authority in colonial hands.

questions.question: A history of World War II describes all Philippine guerrillas as following one nationwide command and political program. Which evidence would most directly challenge that account?

choices.A: Evidence of occupation across several provinces would not establish a single command or shared political program.
choices.B: An account describing how one unit operated and obtained supplies in a particular province.
choices.C: A photograph documenting captured weapons or uniforms used by one guerrilla unit.
choices.D: Records show distinct regional leaders, Allied ties, and local aims among guerrilla groups.

questions.note: Resistance groups varied by region, leadership, ideology, military connection, and local purpose; they were not one uniform organization.

questions.question: Two constitutions adopted during crises both promise civil liberties, but only one is effectively enforced. What should a historian compare to explain the difference?

choices.A: Compare how clearly each document describes civil liberties and the language used to promise them.
choices.B: Compare institutional powers, participation, enforcement practices, and remedies for violations.
choices.C: Compare the drafting dates and political crisis each document followed, without examining enforcement.
choices.D: Compare the documents’ length and number of signatures as indicators of how seriously rights were treated.

questions.note: Constitutional text must be read alongside institutional capacity, enforcement, political conditions, and actual access to remedies.

questions.question: After the Suez Canal opened in 1869, travel between the Philippines and Europe became faster. Which development most directly connected this change to the Propaganda Movement?

choices.A: It made travel from the Philippines to the United States much faster, connecting reformists to American political groups.
choices.B: It reduced travel time to Europe but chiefly redirected Filipino students toward commercial training in Cuba.
choices.C: The canal made travel and communication easier for some Filipino reformists in Europe.
choices.D: It improved travel inside Spain while leaving the journey between Asia and Europe largely unchanged.

questions.note: Faster routes helped some ilustrados travel, study, and circulate reform arguments, though the canal alone did not cause nationalism.

questions.question: Manila opened to world trade in 1834, and the Manila–Acapulco Galleon Trade ended in 1815. What does the chronology imply?

choices.A: The end of the galleon trade preceded Manila’s broader opening to world commerce
choices.B: The galleon route ended after Manila’s 1834 opening, as overseas competition grew later in the century.
choices.C: Manila’s opening in 1834 caused the last galleon voyage to occur almost two decades earlier.
choices.D: The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and therefore explains changes to the galleon trade decades earlier.

questions.note: The last galleon sailed in 1815; Manila’s opening to wider world trade followed in 1834, and the Suez Canal opened in 1869.

questions.question: A historian argues that the Katipunan was exposed because its mass membership made secrecy impossible. Which evidence-based response is strongest?

choices.A: Treat the account as definitive because it identifies one person, without checking whether other sources corroborate it.
choices.B: Patiño’s disclosure is one specific account of an information leak that must be weighed against other evidence.
choices.C: Military setbacks likely affected the organization, so the disclosure account can be set aside as secondary.
choices.D: The size of the organization made secrecy difficult, so the specific circumstances of its discovery add little to the explanation.

questions.note: The discovery of the Katipunan involved specific accounts of disclosure; organizational scale alone cannot settle which factors led authorities to learn of it.

questions.question: American-period public schooling expanded literacy and teacher training, while English and civic curricula also served colonial aims. Which interpretation best fits the two effects?

choices.A: Schooling widened literacy, while its language and civics curriculum remained separate from colonial goals.
choices.B: Schooling widened access while promoting colonial language and civic values.
choices.C: Curriculum design remained largely separate from the priorities of the colonial government.
choices.D: Schools could affect literacy, but language policy had little bearing on political identity.

questions.note: Education can create skills and opportunities while also advancing the language, institutions, and political priorities of the governing power.

questions.question: During the Commonwealth period, public institutions expanded. Which measure would best test whether this expansion made government more inclusive?

choices.A: Count new offices and compare their responsibilities with the populations they serve.
choices.B: Measure whether staffing diversity increased, without examining who can access services or make decisions.
choices.C: Who could access services, who held decision-making power, and which groups remained excluded
choices.D: Compare official descriptions of programs over time, rather than looking at access and outcomes.

questions.note: Counting institutions does not show who benefited; access, representation, implementation, and persistent inequalities are needed to judge inclusion.

questions.question: A memoir published decades after the Philippine Revolution contradicts a contemporary document about a leader’s decision. What is the best next step?

choices.A: Prefer the memoir because later recollection usually becomes more accurate with time.
choices.B: Treat the contradiction as proof that the event cannot be reconstructed reliably.
choices.C: Compare context, incentives, and independent corroboration before revising the interpretation.
choices.D: Retain the contemporary document as conclusive unless its date or authorship can be disproved.

questions.note: Neither age nor retrospective perspective guarantees accuracy; provenance, purpose, context, and corroboration matter.

questions.question: During American rule, Filipino officials could win local elections while U.S. authorities retained control over national sovereignty. What political effect could this arrangement have?

choices.A: It shifted influence toward appointed U.S. administrators and away from Filipino local elites.
choices.B: It transferred national authority over foreign affairs while leaving municipal services under colonial supervision.
choices.C: It encouraged local electoral contests but made patronage and public services irrelevant to building political support.
choices.D: It enabled some local leaders to build political influence without full national self-rule

questions.note: Limited electoral participation could build local political careers and networks even while colonial control over sovereignty persisted.

questions.question: To explain Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, a historian examines media closures, arrests, changes in the legislature, and weakening of judicial checks. Why is this broader than a list of individual abuses?

choices.A: It assumes institutions changed together because one declaration affected them all.
choices.B: It examines institutional conditions that enabled, normalized, or concealed abuses over time.
choices.C: It centers the explanation on the proclamation and treats later institutional change as a consequence.
choices.D: It makes individual experiences irrelevant to historical explanation.

questions.note: Institutional changes help explain how power was exercised and sustained, complementing rather than replacing evidence about individual experiences.

questions.question: A newly discovered letter appears to show that a revolutionary leader changed a decision earlier than historians believed. Which approach is strongest?

choices.A: Revise the interpretation as soon as an authenticated letter conflicts with the accepted account.
choices.B: Give the letter priority because it is newer evidence than the sources used by earlier historians.
choices.C: Reject the letter because established interpretations should not change without official approval.
choices.D: Verify the letter’s date and provenance, then compare it with independent evidence.

questions.note: New evidence can revise chronology or motive, but only after provenance, authenticity, context, and corroboration are checked.

questions.question: A national monument presents a hero as consistently committed to one political goal, while the hero’s letters show changing views over time. What should a historian do?

choices.A: Use the letters to trace changing views beyond the monument’s fixed image.
choices.B: Treat letters as private and unrepresentative evidence unless their claims are compared with other writings.
choices.C: Read every change of view as opportunism, even when the letters show changes in events or political conditions.
choices.D: Favor the monument because public commemorations usually capture a person’s views more accurately than private letters.

questions.note: Commemoration often simplifies a life; dated correspondence can help show change, context, and the limits of a single heroic narrative.

questions.question: A large crowd gathers in Manila for a political event, and organizers call it “the will of the entire nation.” Which evidence would best test that claim?

choices.A: Compare turnout with Manila’s registered voters to infer how much of the capital supported the claim.
choices.B: Participation across regions and social groups, along with dissent and barriers to participation
choices.C: Use contemporary polling and news coverage in Manila as a proxy for opinion across the country.
choices.D: Compare turnout with a later national election result, treating the result as a direct measure of the event’s participants.

questions.note: A mass gathering can be significant without representing every region, class, or political position; wider evidence tests the scope of the claim.

questions.question: The Tejeros Convention and later conflict among revolutionary leaders involved both regional rivalries and disputes over authority. Which explanation best accounts for the conflict?

choices.A: Competing leadership claims interacted with regional loyalties and disagreements over revolutionary governance.
choices.B: Regional loyalties mattered, but the factions agreed on the convention’s outcome and accepted the same authority structure.
choices.C: The dispute concerned voting procedure alone, with little connection to competing claims over revolutionary leadership.
choices.D: The divisions mainly reflected different views of negotiations with Spain, rather than regional ties or authority.

questions.note: Disputes at Tejeros reflected questions of authority and representation alongside regional divisions and military priorities.

questions.question: A claim says that outside contact with the Philippine archipelago began only when Magellan arrived in 1521. Which finding would most directly challenge that claim?

choices.A: Pre-1521 finds and records link Philippine communities with neighboring Asian ports.
choices.B: Spanish administrative reports describe new colonial settlements established after the 1560s.
choices.C: Records show that Manila became a major center of colonial administration under Spanish rule.
choices.D: Nineteenth-century reformers traveled through Europe and circulated political writings there.

questions.note: Evidence of contact with neighboring Asian ports before 1521 directly challenges the claim that outside contact began with Magellan. The other evidence concerns later colonial or reform-period developments.

questions.question: A land-reform program distributes some land titles, yet tenants remain dependent on creditors and buyers who set prices. What evidence best tests whether agrarian power actually changed?

choices.A: Compare average plot size before and after reform, without examining debt or tenants’ bargaining power.
choices.B: Count the titles distributed by the program, treating legal ownership as equivalent to control over rural markets.
choices.C: Survey landowners about reform, without measuring tenants’ contracts or dependence on creditors.
choices.D: Test changes in landholding alongside debt, contracts, bargaining power, and market access before and after reform.

questions.note: Land titles may alter legal ownership without fully changing debt, market dependence, or labor relations; outcomes should be traced across these dimensions.

questions.question: After independence in 1946, the Philippines remained linked to the United States through trade rules, security ties, and economic influence. Which conclusion best distinguishes sovereignty from autonomy?

choices.A: Any continuing trade or security agreement means a state has not attained formal sovereignty.
choices.B: Formal sovereignty can coexist with constraints from unequal trade, security, and financial relationships.
choices.C: Formal independence prevents foreign economic relationships from influencing national policy choices.
choices.D: Economic dependence automatically makes legal sovereignty invalid whenever a stronger country has leverage.

questions.note: Legal independence is distinct from the degree of practical freedom a state has in economic and foreign-policy decisions.

questions.question: A national archive contains many official records but few documents from rural tenants and women. What is the strongest inference from this imbalance?

choices.A: The lack of records suggests that these groups played only a secondary role in political and social change.
choices.B: A large collection of official documents can represent society’s experience even when private voices are scarce.
choices.C: Official records can be treated as representative once they cover several regions, even if other groups are underdocumented.
choices.D: The archive reflects unequal preservation; other evidence is needed for underdocumented groups.

questions.note: Archival silence can reflect who had access to writing, institutions, and preservation; it does not prove absent groups were historically inactive.

questions.question: A court record, an oral account, and a material artifact suggest different dates for a local uprising. Which method best handles the conflict?

choices.A: Choose the date that appears most often in state records, because repetition independently confirms accuracy.
choices.B: Assess provenance, purpose, dating methods, and independent corroboration before explaining the mismatch.
choices.C: Prefer the oral account because memory preserves event dates more faithfully than written records.
choices.D: Average the dates into a compromise estimate instead of investigating how each source was produced.

questions.note: Different evidence types have distinct strengths; source criticism should explain discrepancies instead of mechanically choosing or averaging them.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to analyze Martial Law in the Philippines as an unchanging period from 1972 to 1981?

choices.A: The formal lifting of Martial Law in 1981 marked a political transition, so earlier patterns of repression are no longer relevant to later developments.
choices.B: Institutions, opposition, economic conditions, and political pressures changed over the period.
choices.C: Changes in the legal status of Martial Law explain the period more fully than shifts in political practice or opposition.
choices.D: Because the same president remained in power, changes in repression and economic pressure are best treated as background rather than historical developments.

questions.note: Periodization helps examine shifts within authoritarian rule, including changes in institutions, opposition, policy, and public pressure.

questions.question: A later revolutionary victory is used to claim that all participants from the beginning shared the same goal. What reasoning error does this risk?

choices.A: Assuming later outcomes prove that every earlier participant intended that outcome
choices.B: Inferring every member’s personal motive from one prominent leader’s public statements.
choices.C: Treating the movement’s later success as proof that all early participants shared identical social backgrounds.
choices.D: Assuming that a sequence of events proves the first event directly caused the final outcome.

questions.note: This is teleological reasoning: later outcomes are projected backward as if they had been inevitable and universally intended.

questions.question: Spanish, English, and Filipino language policies have each shaped schooling and public life in different periods. What is the strongest historical inference?

choices.A: An official language usually represents the language spoken by most residents and therefore reduces political inequality.
choices.B: Language policy mostly changes classroom vocabulary, while access to state institutions remains unaffected.
choices.C: Language policy can shape access to schooling and government while privileging political identities.
choices.D: Adopting a common official language tends to remove regional inequality without changes in resources or representation.

questions.note: Language is linked to education, administration, social mobility, and national identity, but policies affect groups differently.

questions.question: A leader’s decision precedes a major political change, but labor movements, institutions, and international pressure also shifted. What evidence would best test whether the leader alone caused the change?

choices.A: Compare institutions, collective action, and cases where the leader had less influence.
choices.B: Count later biographies that praise the leader, without checking their sources or purpose.
choices.C: Confirm the leader held office at the time and set aside other changes happening in parallel.
choices.D: Use the leader’s reform speech as proof that the change depended on that person alone.

questions.note: Causal attribution requires testing the leader’s role against structural conditions, collective action, and alternative explanations.

questions.question: An election is held under a constitution, but opponents face intimidation and media access is uneven. Why should legal constitutionality and democratic legitimacy be assessed separately?

choices.A: Following formal rules alone does not ensure free competition, meaningful participation, or freedom from coercion.
choices.B: Legal regularity is sufficient to establish legitimacy unless the official vote count is disputed.
choices.C: Unequal media access affects campaign fairness, while intimidation matters only if ballots are changed.
choices.D: High turnout is the strongest indicator of legitimacy even when opposition access and freedom from coercion are uneven.

questions.note: Formal legality matters, but legitimacy also depends on conditions that allow meaningful, free, and fair participation.

questions.question: During World War II, the Commonwealth government continued in exile while Japanese occupation authorities exercised power inside the Philippines. Which conclusion best distinguishes legal continuity from control on the ground?

choices.A: The Commonwealth maintained ordinary governing authority throughout occupied communities while its leaders were in exile.
choices.B: The occupation ended the Commonwealth’s legal existence because the capital and territory were under Japanese control.
choices.C: The government could continue legally in exile while losing practical control inside occupied territory.
choices.D: Japanese occupation transferred internationally recognized sovereignty to Japan for the remainder of the war.

questions.note: The Commonwealth government continued under Quezon and later Osmeña in exile, while Japanese occupation disrupted authority and daily administration in the islands.
